label: d:rationality
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{d:rationality}
     We say that $[\alpha]$ is \textit{rational} if $\mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})\cong \mathbb{Z}$, and $[\alpha]$ is \textit{irrational} if $\mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z}) = \{0\}$.
head: environment

label: d:prmitive length
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{d:prmitive length}
     If $[\alpha]$ is rational, there exists a unique generator $v$ of $\mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})$ such that $[\alpha]=\ell v$ for a unique constant $\ell >0$. We call $\ell=:\ell([\alpha]) $ the \textit{primitive length} of $[\alpha]$. If $[\alpha]$ is irrational, we define the primitive length $\ell([\alpha])=0$ in view of the fact that $\mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z}) = \{0\}$.
head: environment

label: r:remark_on_the_rationality
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{r:remark_on_the_rationality}
     When $[\alpha] = 0$, i.e. $\alpha$ is exact, we also define $\ell([\alpha])=0$. Note that we don't say that $[\alpha]$ is irrational in this case since Definition~\ref{d:rationality} requires $[\alpha]\neq0$ (cf. Remark~\ref{r:lott.sesum}).

label: d:pointed.cinfty.convergence
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{d:pointed.cinfty.convergence}
Let $\{(M_i, g_i(t),\alpha_i(t), p_i)\}_{i=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of families of metrics and closed 1-forms defined on pointed manifolds $(M_i,p_i)$ for $t \in (0,\infty)$. We say that
\[
(M_i, g_i(t),\alpha_i(t), p_i) \xrightarrow{pt\ C^\infty} (M_\infty, g_\infty(t),\alpha_\infty(t), p_\infty)
\]
if there exist:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item An exhaustion $\{U_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ of $M_\infty$ with $p_\infty \in U_j$;
    
    \item Open subsets $V_{i,j} \subset M_i$ with $p_i \in V_{i,j}$ and diffeomorphisms
    \[
    \phi_{i,j} : U_j \to V_{i,j}, \qquad \phi_{i,j}(p_\infty)=p_i;
    \]
    
    \item For all $j$,
    \[
    \phi_{i,j}^* g_i(t) \to g_\infty(t), \qquad \phi_{i,j}^* \alpha_i(t) \to \alpha_\infty(t)
    \]
    smoothly on $U_j \times [j^{-1},j]$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Pointed $C^\infty$ (Cheeger--Gromov) convergence

label: d:equivariant.pointed.cinfty.convergence
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{d:equivariant.pointed.cinfty.convergence}
In addition to the above, suppose that $G_i$ acts isometrically on $(M_i,g_i(1))$ and preserves $\alpha_i(1)$. For $l>0$, write
\[
G_i(l):=\{\gamma\in G_i : d_{g_i(1)}(\gamma p_i,p_i)\le l\}.
\]

We say that
\[
(M_i, g_i(1),\alpha_i(1),G_i, p_i) \xrightarrow{pt\ eq\ C^\infty} (M_\infty, g_\infty(1),\alpha_\infty(1),G_\infty, p_\infty)
\]
if:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $(M_i, g_i(t),\alpha_i(t), p_i) \xrightarrow{pt\ C^\infty} (M_\infty, g_\infty(t),\alpha_\infty(t), p_\infty)$ with maps $\phi_{i,j}$ as above;

    \item $G_\infty \subset \mathrm{Isom}(M_\infty,g_\infty(1))$ is a closed subgroup preserving $\alpha_\infty(1)$;

    \item For every $j$ and all sufficiently large $i$, there exist maps
    \[
    \varphi_{i,j} : G_i(j) \to G_\infty(j+1), \qquad \psi_{i,j} : G_\infty(j) \to G_i(j+1),
    \]
    such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
        \item For every $\gamma \in G_i(j)$ and $x \in U_j$ with $\gamma(\phi_{i,j}(x)) \in V_{i,j}$,
        \[
        d_{g_\infty(1)}\big(\phi_{i,j}^{-1}(\gamma(\phi_{i,j}(x))), \varphi_{i,j}(\gamma)(x)\big) \to 0;
        \]
        
        \item For every $\eta \in G_\infty(j)$ and $x \in U_j$ with $\psi_{i,j}(\eta)(\phi_{i,j}(x)) \in V_{i,j}$,
        \[
        d_{g_\infty(1)}\big(\phi_{i,j}^{-1}(\psi_{i,j}(\eta)(\phi_{i,j}(x))), \eta(x)\big) \to 0;
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
    as $i \to \infty$, uniformly over the indicated group elements and points $x\in U_j$ satisfying the respective conditions.
\end{enumerate}

By \cite[Theorem 2-1]{fukaya1986theory}, if $(M_i, g_i(1),\alpha_i(1), p_i) \xrightarrow{pt\ eq\ C^\infty} (M_\infty, g_\infty(1),\alpha_\infty(1), p_\infty)$, then we have $(M_i/G_i, d_{g_i(1)})\to (M_\infty/G_\infty,d_{g_\infty(1)})$ in Gromov--Hausdorff topology with the following commutative diagram\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
  & (M_i, g_i(1),\alpha_i(1), G_i, p_i) 
  \arrow[r, "pt\ eq\ C^\infty"] 
  \arrow[d, "\pi_{i}"]
   & (M_\infty, g_\infty(1),\alpha_\infty(1),G_\infty, p_\infty) 
   \arrow[d, "\pi_\infty"]\\
  & (M_i/G_i, d_{g_i(1)})
  \arrow[r, "GH"]
   & (M_\infty/G_\infty,d_{g_\infty(1)}).
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

title: Notation
body_md:
To simplify our notation, we write $(M,g_s(1))\xrightarrow{GH} (X,d)$ if $(M,g_s(1))$ converges to $(X,d)$ in Gromov--Hausdorff sense as $s\to\infty$.
Moreover, we write $(\tilde g_s(t),\tilde \alpha_s(t))\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(\tilde g_\infty(t),\tilde \alpha_\infty(t))$ 
to denote the pointed Cheeger-Gromov convergence on the universal cover.
If we replace $s$ by $s_i$, then the above convergences are along the sequence $s_i\to\infty$.

label: r:lott.sesum
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{r:lott.sesum}
    Lott and Sesum’s result \cite{lott2014ricci} treats the case $[\alpha]=0$, where $(M,g(t))$ converges to a flat $2$-torus and hence $(M,t^{-1}g(t))$ collapses to a point and $(\tilde g_s(t),\tilde \alpha_s(t))\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(g_{\mathrm{Euc}},0)$ as $s\to\infty$. In our case where $[\alpha]\neq 0$, the limit on the universal cover is $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$, which is different from $(g_{\mathrm{Euc}},0)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: We note that in case (i), the conclusion implies $\alpha^*(\partial_v)=0$ since $\alpha^*=\sqrt 2 d\theta$, which means $\alpha^*$ has no component in the fiber direction of the action $G_\infty$. This fact plays an important role in showing the full sequence convergence both in Gromov--Hausdorff sense and on the universal cover (cf. Theorem~\ref{no_fiber_component}).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: We want to compare our result with the result of Lott \cite{lott2010dimensional,lott2026under} where he showed that compact 3-dimensional Type III Ricci flow has similar collapsing behavior determined by the Thurston type of the manifold. Our result can be viewed as a generalization to noncompact manifolds with symmetry determined by $[\alpha]$ in view of the warped product interpretation in Section~\ref{intro}. In our case, the collapsing behavior also depends on the topology, namely the cohomology class $[\alpha]$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Theorem~\ref{t:main.GH_limit} exhibits a new type of metric behavior in a geometric flow, despite the many formal similarities between the Ricci flow and \eqref{alpha_Ricci_flow}. In particular, the long-time behavior depends on the arithmetic property of the initial data. As $[\alpha]$ varies, the long-time behavior changes dramatically. We expect that analogous phenomena occur for higher-dimensional tori as well.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The metric component of the $\alpha$-Ricci flow \eqref{alpha_Ricci_flow} is not conformal. When the initial metric is flat and the $1$-form is parallel, one can show that the conformal class $[g(t)] \in \mathbb{H}^2 / \operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ converges to $\left[\left(\frac{a}{b}, 0\right)\right] \in \partial \mathbb{H}^2 / \operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ where $a,b$ are the periods of $\alpha$ on a set of generators of $\pi_1(M)$ (cf.\ the proof of Theorem~\ref{model.case}).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In the irrational case, our method only gives a subsequence $s_i\to\infty$ such that the desired convergences hold. It would be desirable to show that the convergences are along the full sequence.

label: p:equivalent definition
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove (i), let $[\gamma_1]^*,[\gamma_2]^*\in H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})$ be the dual basis of $[\gamma_1],[\gamma_2]\in H_1(M,\mathbb{Z})$. 
    Suppose $[\alpha]$ is rational. Then there exists $c>0$ such that:
    \begin{align*}
        c[\alpha] = m[\gamma_1]^* +n[\gamma_2]^*,
    \end{align*}
    for some integers $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, we have $a = m/c$ and $b = n/c$. Hence $a/b = m/n\in \mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$.  
    
    Now suppose $a/b\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$. If $a,b\neq0$, then there exist $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ such that $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{p}{q}$, with $\operatorname{gcd}(p,q) = 1$ and $p/a = q/b = c$, for some constant $c$. Thus, $c[\alpha] = p[\gamma_1]^*+q[\gamma_2]^*$, which shows that $[\alpha]$ is rational. If $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, then we can choose $c = b^{-1}$ or $a^{-1}$ to see that $[\alpha]$ is rational.
    
    To prove (ii), by definition of $a,b,[\gamma_1]^*,[\gamma_2]^*$, we have $[\alpha] = a[\gamma_1]^* +b[\gamma_2]^*$. If $a/b\in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then by definition $\ell([\alpha])=\ell_{a,b}=0$. If $a/b\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$ and $a,b\neq0$, there exist $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ such that $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{p}{q}$ with $\operatorname{gcd}(p,q) = 1$. We have \[(\ell_{a,b})^{-1}[\alpha]=\operatorname{sign}(a)|p|[\gamma_1]^*+\operatorname{sign}(b)|q|[\gamma_2]^*\in H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})\] and\begin{align*}
        \mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})=&\{c[\alpha]:ca\in \mathbb{Z},cb\in \mathbb{Z}\}\\
        =&\{c'(\ell_{a,b})^{-1}[\alpha]:c'\operatorname{sign}(a)|p|\in \mathbb{Z},c'\operatorname{sign}(b)|q|\in \mathbb{Z} \}\\
        =&\{c'(\ell_{a,b})^{-1}[\alpha]:c'\in\mathbb{Z}\},
    \end{align*} where we substitute $\ell_{a,b}c=c'$ in the second equality and use $\gcd(p,q)=1$ in the third equality. Thus $\mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}\cdot [(\ell_{a,b})^{-1}\alpha]$ and $[\alpha]=\ell_{a,b}[(\ell_{a,b})^{-1}\alpha]$. If $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, then $\mathbb{R}\cdot[\alpha]\cap H^1(M,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}\cdot[\gamma_2]^*$ or $\mathbb{Z}\cdot[\gamma_1]^*$ and $[\alpha]= \ell_{a,b}(\operatorname{sign}(b) [\gamma_2]^*)$ or $ \ell_{a,b}(\operatorname{sign}(a) [\gamma_1]^*)$. In any case, $\ell([\alpha])=\ell_{a,b}$.

body_md:
Let $\tilde\gamma_1$ be a lift of $\gamma_1$ to $\tilde M$ such that $\tilde\gamma_1(0)=x$ and $\tilde\gamma_1(1)=[\gamma_1](x)$. Then \[u([\gamma_1](x))-u(x)=\int _{\tilde\gamma_1} du(\tilde\gamma_1')=\int_{\gamma_1}\alpha=a.\] In particular, $[\gamma_1]$ maps $u^{-1}(r)$ to $u^{-1}(r+a)$ for any $r\in\mathbb{R}$. The case for $[\gamma_2]$ is similar. 

    If $[\alpha]$ is rational, by an algebraic fact, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\{u^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-action generated by $u^{-1}(r)\mapsto u^{-1}(r+\ell_{a,b})$ and $\ell_{a,b}=\ell([\alpha])$ by Proposition~\ref{p:equivalent definition}. 
    
    If $[\alpha]$ is irrational, by an algebraic fact, then the action has dense orbits.

body_md:

An example relevant to this paper is given by

(M, g, \alpha, f) = (\mathbb{R}^N, g_{\mathrm{Euc}}, 0, -\tfrac{1}{4}|v|^2),$

head: environment

label: example.noncompact invariant expander
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example.noncompact invariant expander}
Consider $(M,g,\alpha,f) = (\mathbb{R}^N\times\mathbb{R}, g_{\mathbb{R}^N}+ d\theta^2, \sqrt{2}d\theta,-\frac{1}{4}|v|^2)$ where $v$ denotes the standard coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $\theta$ denotes the standard coordinate on $\mathbb{R}$. One can check that this is a gradient $\alpha$-Ricci expander. We write $\phi_t(\theta,v) = (\theta,t^{-\frac{1}{2}}v)$ for the one parameter family of diffeomorphisms generated by $\frac{1}{t}\nabla f$. Then \begin{align*}
    g^*(t) &=t\phi_t^*g= g_{\mathbb{R}^N} + td\theta^2\\
    \alpha^*(t) &=\phi_t^*\alpha= \sqrt{2}d\theta\equiv \alpha^*
\end{align*} is an $\alpha$-Ricci flow on $(0,\infty)$.
Since $\alpha^*(t)$ is spatially constant and $g^*(t)$ is flat, one can view 
$(g^*(t), \alpha^*(t))$ as an $\alpha$-Ricci flow on any quotient of 
$\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$, for example, on $S^1\times\mathbb{R}^N$.
The case relevant to this paper is $N=1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: When converted back to the usual Ricci flow by taking a warped product with $\mathbb{R}$ (cf. section \ref{intro}), the expander $(g^*(t), \alpha^*(t))$ is isometric to $\mathbb{R}^{N}\times \mathbb{H}^2$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The behavior of $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ is that the base metric on $S^1$ expands while the fiber metric on $\mathbb{R}^N$ remains fixed. This resembles the expander on the Sol-geometry in the 3D-Ricci flow \cite[Section 3.3.2]{lott2007long}. This also indicates that with the presence of $\alpha$, the long-time behavior of the $\alpha$-Ricci flow is determined not only by the curvature of $g$, which is flat for all $t$, but also by $\alpha$.

label: l:R2.invariant.solution
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:R2.invariant.solution}
    Let $(\tilde g(t), \tilde \alpha(t))$ be a solution to the $\alpha$-Ricci flow on $\mathbb{R}^2 \times (0,\infty)$ 
which is invariant under translations of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Then either $(\tilde g(t), \tilde \alpha(t))$ 
is isometric to $(g^*(t+c), \alpha^*(t+c))$ for some $c \ge 0$, or it is the static solution 
$(g_{\mathrm{Euc}}, 0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $(\tilde g(t), \tilde \alpha(t))$ is translation invariant, we have $\tilde g(t)$ is flat for $t\in (0,\infty)$ and $\tilde\alpha(t)$ is parallel with respect to $\tilde g(t)$. By \eqref{alpha_Ricci_flow}, $\tilde \alpha(t)\equiv\tilde\alpha$ is constant in time. If $\tilde\alpha=0$, then integrating \eqref{alpha_Ricci_flow} shows that $\tilde g(t)$ is isometric to $g_{\mathrm{Euc}}$. If $\tilde\alpha\neq0$, we choose coordinates $(\theta,v)$ such that $\tilde g(1)(\partial_v,\partial_\theta)=0$, $\tilde\alpha=\sqrt{2}d\theta$ and $\tilde g(1)=dv^2+\frac{c_0}{2}\tilde\alpha\otimes\tilde\alpha$ for some $c_0>0$. Integrating \eqref{alpha_Ricci_flow}, we get $\tilde  g(t)=dv^2+\frac{t-1+c_0}{2}\tilde\alpha\otimes \tilde \alpha$. Since $\tilde g(t)$ is a metric for $t\in (0,\infty)$, we have $c=c_0-1\ge0$. Thus $\tilde  g(t)=dv^2+\frac{t+c}{2}\tilde\alpha\otimes \tilde \alpha=g^*(t+c)$ and $\tilde \alpha(t)=\alpha^*(t+c)$.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{l:R2.invariant.solution}, there is $c\ge 0$ such that in some coordinates $(\theta,v)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ we have \[(\tilde{g}(t),\tilde{\alpha}(t))=(g^*(t+c),\alpha^*(t+c))=(dv^2+\frac{t+c}{2}\alpha^*\otimes \alpha^*,\alpha^*=\sqrt 2d\theta).\] Consider the blow-down solution \[\tilde{g}_s(t) = \frac{1}{s}\tilde{g}(st)=\frac{1}{s}dv^2 + \frac{(st+c)}{2s}\alpha^*\otimes\alpha^*,\quad\tilde{\alpha}_s(t) \equiv \alpha^*.\] Let $\psi_s(\theta,v)=(\theta,s^{\frac{1}{2}}v)$. Then as $s\to\infty$, we have
\[\psi_s^*\tilde g_s(t)=dv^2 + \frac{(st+c)}{2s}\alpha^*\otimes\alpha^*\to g^*(t),\quad \psi_s^*\tilde \alpha_s(t)\equiv\alpha^*.\]This finishes the proof.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{model.case}
	Let $(g(t),\alpha(t))$ be a solution to the $\alpha$-Ricci flow on $\mathbb{T}^2$ with $g(0)$ flat and $\alpha(0)$ nonzero and parallel with respect to $g(0)$. Then we have the following.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item If $[\alpha]$ is rational, then $(M,t^{-1}g(t))\xrightarrow{GH}(S^1,d([\alpha]))$ as $t\to\infty$. Moreover, we have $d_{GH}((M,t^{-1}g(t)),(S^1,d([\alpha])))=O(t^{-1/2})$.
		\item If $[\alpha]$ is irrational, then  $(M,t^{-1}g(t))\xrightarrow{GH}\{\mathrm{pt}\}$ as $t\to\infty$.
	\end{enumerate}
    In either case, on the universal cover, we have $(\tilde g_s(t),\tilde \alpha_s(t))\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ as $s\to\infty$.

label: gcd
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider the fundamental domain $F_t$ of the lattice generated by $e_1(t)$, $e_2(t)$:
	\[F_t=\{c_1e_1(t)+c_2e_2(t):0\le c_1,c_2\le 1\}.\] 
    It suffices to show that for any $p\in F_t$, $d_t(p,S_\ell):=\inf_{0\le c\le \ell}d_t(p,\frac{c}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta)\le Ct^{-1/2}$.
	Any point $p\in F_t$ can be written as $p=\frac{x}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta+\frac{y}{\sqrt 2}\partial_v$ for some $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. By \eqref{est1} and \eqref{est2}, we have
	\[0\le x\le a+b,\quad |y|=O(t^{-1/2}).\]
	We write $x=\lfloor x/\ell\rfloor \ell+\{x/\ell\}\ell$ where $\lfloor x/\ell\rfloor$ is the integer part of $x/\ell$ and $\{x/\ell\}$ is the fractional part of $x/\ell$.
	Then we have
    \begin{align*}
	d_t\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta+\frac{y}{\sqrt 2}\partial_v,S_\ell\right)
	\le&d_t\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta+\frac{y}{\sqrt 2}\partial_v,
	\frac{\{x/\ell\}\ell}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta\right)\\
    \le&d_{t^{-1}\tilde g(t)}\left(
    \frac{x}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta+\frac{y}{\sqrt 2}\partial_v
    ,\frac{\{x/\ell\}\ell}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta
    +r\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\ell}\right\rfloor e_1(t)
    +s\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\ell}\right\rfloor e_2(t)\right)\\
    \le&(1+Ct^{-1/2})\left|
    \frac{x}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta+\frac{y}{\sqrt 2}\partial_v
    -\frac{\{x/\ell\}\ell}{\sqrt 2}\partial_\theta
    -r\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\ell}\right\rfloor e_1(t)
    -s\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\ell}\right\rfloor e_2(t)
    \right|\\
	\le&
	(1+Ct^{-1/2})\left|\left\lfloor \frac{x}{\ell} \right\rfloor\right|
	\left|
	\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
	-r\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
	-s\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
	\right|
	+(1+Ct^{-1/2})\left|\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_v\right|\\
    &\quad+(1+Ct^{-1/2})
    \left|\left\lfloor \frac{x}{\ell} \right\rfloor\right|
    \left(
    |r|\left|e_1(t)-\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta\right|
    +|s|\left|e_2(t)-\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta\right|
    \right)\\
	\le&Ct^{-1/2}.
\end{align*}

label: epsilon
title: Proof
body_md:
First, we show (i). By Proposition~\ref{p:equivalent definition}, $[\alpha]$ is rational if and only if $\frac{a}{b}\in \mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$. If $a,b>0$ and $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{p}{q}$ where $\gcd (p,q)=1$, then there exist $r,s\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $r p+s q=1$ and hence $ra+sb=\frac{b}{q}=\ell_{a,b}$. If $a=0$ and $b>0$, then $0a+1b=b= \ell_{a,b}$. If $b=0$ and $a>0$, then $1a+0b=a= \ell_{a,b}$. In any case, we can apply Lemma~\ref{gcd} with $\ell=\ell_{a,b}$ and $r,s,a,b$ as above to get 
	\begin{equation}\label{epsilon}
		(M,t^{-1}g(t))\text{ is contained in a } Ct^{-1/2} \text{ neighborhood of }\pi(S_\ell).
	\end{equation}
    Now, we show that  there is $C=C(\ell,r,s,a,b,g(0))$ such that for any $0\le x,y\le 1$,
\begin{equation}\label{e:metric.on.S.ell}
	\left|d_t\left(
	\frac{x\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta,
	\frac{y\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
	\right)
	-
	\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\rho(x,y)\right|\le Ct^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}
	where $\rho$ is the standard metric on $S^1=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ of length 1. 

Let $|\cdot|$ denote the standard Euclidean norm in the $(\theta,v)$ coordinates. For $p_1,p_2\in \mathbb{R}^2$ we define
\begin{align*}
d_E\left(
p_1,
p_2
\right)\
=
\min_{m_1,m_2\in\mathbb Z}
\left|
p_1-p_2-m_1e_1(t)-m_2e_2(t)
\right|.
\end{align*}
Then by \eqref{est1} and \eqref{est2},
\begin{align*}
d_E\left(
\frac{x\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta,
\frac{y\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
\right)=\min_{m_1,m_2\in \mathbb{Z}}\left|
\frac{(x-y)\ell-m_1a-m_2b}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
+\frac{(m_1b-m_2a)\sqrt {C_0}}{\rho\sqrt t}\partial_v
\right|.
\end{align*}
Since $\partial_\theta$ and $\partial_v$ are orthogonal, for any $m_1,m_2\in\mathbb Z$, we have
$$
\left|
\frac{(x-y)\ell-m_1a-m_2b}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
+\frac{(m_1b-m_2a)\sqrt {C_0}}{\rho\sqrt t}\partial_v
\right|
\ge
\left|
\frac{(x-y)\ell-m_1a-m_2b}{\sqrt{2}}
\right|.
$$
Hence
$$
d_E\left(
\frac{x\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta,
\frac{y\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
\right)
\ge
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\min_{m_1,m_2\in\mathbb Z}
\left|(x-y)\ell-m_1a-m_2b\right|=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt 2}\rho(x,y).
$$
On the other hand, let $n_1,n_2\in\mathbb Z$ be such that
$$
\left|(x-y)\ell-n_1a-n_2b\right|
=
\min_{m_1,m_2\in\mathbb Z}
\left|(x-y)\ell-m_1a-m_2b\right|=\ell\rho(x,y).
$$
Such $(n_1,n_2)$ can be chosen from $(0,0)$ or $\pm (r,s)$.
Then
\begin{align*}
d_E\left(
\frac{x\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta,
\frac{y\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
\right)
&\le
\left|
\frac{(x-y)\ell-n_1a-n_2b}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
+\frac{(n_1b-n_2a)\sqrt {C_0}}{\rho\sqrt t}\partial_v
\right|\\
&\le
\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\rho(x,y)
+Ct^{-1/2}.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
$$
	\left|d_E\left(
	\frac{x\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta,
	\frac{y\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
	\right)
	-
	\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\rho(x,y)\right|\le Ct^{-1/2}.
$$
Since $\left|\frac{\tilde g(t)}{t}-(d\theta^2+dv^2)\right|\le Ct^{-1/2}$, the corresponding distance functions converge uniformly on the relevant fundamental domains. Hence
$$
\left|d_t\left(
\frac{x\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta,
\frac{y\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\partial_\theta
\right)
-
\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2}}\rho(x,y)\right|\le Ct^{-1/2}.
$$

	Thus, we see that $(\pi(S_\ell),t^{-1}g(t))$ converges to the metric space $(S^1,d([\alpha]))$. Combining (\ref{epsilon}) and \eqref{e:metric.on.S.ell}, we get \[d_{GH}((M,t^{-1}g(t)), (S^1,d([\alpha])))=O(t^{-1/2}).\]
	
	Next, we show (ii). Since $\frac{a}{b}\in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, we have $b>0$. For any $0<\epsilon\le2b$ we apply Lemma~\ref{dense} with $\lambda=\frac{a}{b}$, $y=\frac{\epsilon}{2b}$, $\delta=\frac{\epsilon}{4b}$ to obtain $r,s\in \mathbb{Z}$ so that $|\frac{\epsilon}{2b}-r\frac{a}{b}-s|<\frac{\epsilon}{4b}$. Hence $|\frac{\epsilon}{2} -ra-sb|<\epsilon/4$. We apply Lemma~\ref{gcd} with $\ell=ra+sb$ where $\frac{1}{4} \epsilon\le \ell\le \frac{3}{4}\epsilon$. Then we get $(M,t^{-1}g(t))$ is contained in a $C(\epsilon)t^{-1/2}$-neighborhood of $\pi(S_\ell) \subset\pi(S_{3\epsilon/4})$. Since $\operatorname{diam}(\pi(S_{3\epsilon/4}))\le \sqrt{1+\frac{2A_0}{\rho^2t}}\frac{3\epsilon}{4\sqrt 2}$, for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $t_0=t_0(\epsilon)>0$ so that for $t>t_0$, $\operatorname{diam}(M,t^{-1}g(t)) \le \epsilon$. Thus we have $(M,t^{-1}g(t))$ converges to a point in the Gromov--Hausdorff topology.

label: alpha.norm.estimate
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{alpha.norm.estimate}
    Let $(M^n,g(t),\alpha(t))$ be a solution to the $\alpha$-Ricci flow. Then
    \[\frac{d}{dt}|\alpha|^2=\Delta |\alpha|^2-2|\nabla\alpha|^2-\frac{1}{2}|\alpha|^4.\]
    If $M$ is closed, then with $c_0=\sup_{M \times \{0\}} |\alpha|^2$ we have
    \[
\sup_{M \times \{t\}} |\alpha|^2 \le \ \frac{c_0}{1+\tfrac{c_0t}{2}}.\]
head: environment
name: $\alpha$-norm estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows the  arguments in \cite[Lemma 3.2, Lemma 5.6]{list2008evolution} and \cite[(2.15), (2.19)]{lott2014ricci}.
    We recall the Bochner formula for a closed 1-form:
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{1}{2}\Delta |\alpha|^2=&-\langle \Delta_d\alpha,\alpha\rangle+|\nabla\alpha|^2+\operatorname{Ric}(\alpha,\alpha)\\
        =&-\langle dd^*_g\alpha,\alpha\rangle+|\nabla\alpha|^2+\operatorname{Ric}(\alpha,\alpha).
    \end{align*}
    Consequently, we have
    \begin{align*}
	\frac{d}{dt}|\alpha|^2=&-2\langle dd^*_g\alpha,\alpha\rangle+2\operatorname{Ric}(\alpha,\alpha)-\frac{1}{2}|\alpha|^4\\
	=&\Delta|\alpha|^2-2|\nabla\alpha|^2-\frac{1}{2}|\alpha|^4.
\end{align*}
    Applying the maximum principle when $M$ is closed gives
    \[
\sup_{M \times \{t\}} |\alpha|^2 \le \ \frac{c_0}{1+\tfrac{c_0t}{2}}.\]

label: scalar.curvature.monotonicity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{scalar.curvature.monotonicity}
    Let $(M^n,g(t),\alpha(t))$ be a solution to the $\alpha$-Ricci flow on $[0,T]$. We define $R^{ \alpha}=R-\frac{1}{4}|\alpha|^2$ and $\operatorname{Ric}^{\alpha}=\operatorname{Ric} -\frac{1}{4}\alpha\otimes \alpha$. Then we have
    \[
\frac{\partial  R^{ \alpha}}{\partial t} = \Delta  R^{ \alpha} + 2|{\mathrm{Ric}}^{\alpha}|^2+\frac{1}{2}(d^*_g\alpha)^2.
\]
    If $M$ is closed, then for any $t\in (0,T]$
\[
\inf_{M\times\{t\}} R^{\alpha}\ge -\frac{n}{2t}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The evolution equation for $ R^{ \alpha}$ on $M$ is proved in \cite{guo2025alpha}, see also \cite[(2.16)]{lott2014ricci}. If $M$ is closed, then using the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality $|\operatorname{Ric}^\alpha|^2\ge \frac{1}{n}(R^\alpha)^2$ and the maximum principle, we get $
\inf_{M\times\{t\}} R^{\alpha}\ge -\frac{n}{2t}$.

label: volume.estimate
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Volume estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
By a direct computation and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, we have
    \[V'(t)=\int (-R+\frac{1}{4}|\alpha|^2)dV_{g(t)}=\frac{1}{4}\int|\alpha|^2dV_{g(t)}.\]
    Applying Theorem~\ref{alpha.norm.estimate}, we get
    \[0\le V'(t)\le \frac{c_0}{4+2c_0t}V(t).\]
    Integration gives the claimed bounds.

label: type.iii.estimate
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Type III estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof closely follows that of \cite[Proposition 2.10]{lott2014ricci}, using Theorem~\ref{alpha.norm.estimate} in place of \cite[(2.15), (2.19)]{lott2014ricci}. We provide a brief sketch here.


    We first show that there is no finite-time singularity. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is $T<\infty$ such that the flow is singular at $T$. Then by \cite{guo2025alpha}, we have $\lim_{t\to T^-}\sup_{M\times\{t\}}|R|=\infty$. We can choose a sequence $(x_i,t_i)\in M\times [0,T)$ such that $Q_i:=|R(x_i,t_i)|=\sup _{M\times[0,t_i]}|R(x,t)|\to\infty$. Define the rescaled solutions $g_i(t)=Q_i g(t_i+Q_i^{-1}t)$ and $\alpha_i(t)=\alpha(t_i+Q_i^{-1}t)$. By \cite{guo2025alpha}, $(M\times[-Q_it_i,0],(x_i,0),g_i(t),\alpha_i(t))$ converges in the pointed Cheeger-Gromov topology to $(M_\infty\times(-\infty,0],(m_\infty,0),g_\infty(t),\alpha_\infty(t))$, where $(M_\infty,g_{\infty}(t))$ is a $\kappa$-solution in the sense of \cite[\S 11.2]{perelman2002entropy} and $\alpha_\infty=0$. Hence the limit must be $(S^2,g_{S^2})$. This contradicts the assumption that $M=\mathbb{T}^2$.
    
    It remains to show that $|R(x,t)|\le Ct^{-1}$, for $t\geq 1$.
    Suppose otherwise. Then \[\limsup_{t\to\infty}\sup_{M\times\{t\}}t|R|=\infty.\] Choose a sequence $\{T_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ with $\lim_{i\to\infty}T_i=\infty$, and let $(x_i,t_i)\in M\times[0,T_i]$ be such that 
    \[t_i(T_i-t_i)|R(x_i,t_i)|=\sup_{M\times [0,T_i]}t(T_i-t)|R(x,t)|.\]
    Setting $Q_i=|R(x_i,t_i)|$, we consider the rescaled solutions
    \[g_i(t)=Q_i g(t_i+Q_i^{-1}t),\quad \alpha_i(t)=\alpha(t_i+Q_i^{-1}t).\]
    Then $Q_it_i\to\infty$, and $(g_i(t),\alpha_i(t))$ satisfies the $\alpha$-Ricci flow on a time interval $(A_i,\Omega_i)$, where $\lim_{i\to\infty}A_i=-\infty$ and $\lim_{i\to\infty}\Omega_i=\infty$. This can be seen as in \cite[Chapter 8, 5.1]{chow2004ricci}.
    Since $|R_i(x_i,0)|=1$, we can redefine $A_i,\Omega_i$ such that there exists a sequence $\{\gamma_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$, with $\lim_{i\to\infty}\gamma_i=1$ satisfying
    \[\sup_{M\times [A_i,\Omega_i]}|R_i(x,t)|\le \gamma_i.\]
    Following the idea of the proof in \cite[Lemma 2.11]{lott2014ricci}, and applying Theorem~\ref{alpha.norm.estimate},
    there is an $\epsilon>0$ such that $\operatorname{inj} _{(M,g_i(0))}(x_i)\ge \epsilon$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$.
    Taking the pointed limit of $(M\times[A_i,\Omega_i],(x_i,0),g_i(t),\alpha_i(t))$, we obtain a limit $(M_\infty\times\mathbb{R},~(m_\infty,0),g_\infty(t),\alpha_\infty(t))$. By Theorem~\ref{alpha.norm.estimate},
    \[
    \sup_M|\alpha_i(t)|_{g_i(t)}^2
    =Q_i^{-1}\sup_M|\alpha(t_i+Q_i^{-1}t)|_{g(t_i+Q_i^{-1}t)}^2
    \le\frac{2}{Q_it_i+t}\longrightarrow0
    \]
    uniformly on compact time intervals, so $\alpha_\infty=0$. Theorem~\ref{scalar.curvature.monotonicity} also gives $R_i(t)\ge-\frac{1}{Q_it_i+t}$, hence $R_\infty\ge0$. Moreover, we have
    \[|R_i(x_i,0)|=1.\]
    In conclusion, $(M_\infty,g_\infty(t))$ is a complete eternal solution to the Ricci flow with uniformly bounded curvature. Since the spacetime maximum of $R$ is achieved at some point, \cite[Theorem 9.4]{chow2006hamilton} implies that $(M_\infty,g_\infty(t))$ is the cigar soliton. 
    In particular 
    \[\int_{M_\infty}R_{g_\infty(0)}dV_{g_\infty(0)}=4\pi.\]
    For sufficiently large $i$, there exists a subset $S_i\subset M$ such that
    \[\int_{S_i}R_{g(t_i)}dV_{g(t_i)}\ge 3\pi.\]
    On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{scalar.curvature.monotonicity}
    \[\int_{M\setminus S_i}R_{g(t_i)}dV_{g(t_i)}\ge -\frac{1}{t_i} \operatorname{vol}_{g(t_i)}(M\setminus S_i)\ge -\frac{V(t_i)}{t_i}\ge -\frac{C(1+\sqrt{t_i})}{t_i}\to0.\]
    Thus, for sufficiently large $i$, we obtain
    \[\int_MR_{g(t_i)}dV_{g(t_i)}\ge 2\pi,\]
    which contradicts the fact that $\chi(M)= 0$.

label: growth.of.length.of.shortest.curve
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Systolic inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\gamma$ be a closed geodesic representing the homology class $\sigma$ such that $L(\gamma,g(t))=L_\sigma(t)=:L$. Bounding $L_{\sigma}(t+\Delta t)$ by the length of $\gamma$ at time $t+\Delta t$, we obtain
    \[\limsup_{\Delta t\to0+}\frac{L_\sigma(t+\Delta t)-L_\sigma(t)}{\Delta t}\le\frac{1}{2}\int_0^L\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}(\gamma',\gamma')ds=\int_0^L-\frac{1}{2}R+\frac{1}{4}(\alpha(\gamma'))^2ds.\]
    Similarly, bounding $L_{\sigma}(t-\Delta t)$ by the length of $\gamma$ at time $t-\Delta t$ gives
    \[D_-L_\sigma(t):=\liminf_{\Delta t\to0+}\frac{L_\sigma(t)-L_\sigma(t-\Delta t)}{\Delta t}\ge\int_0^L-\frac{1}{2}R+\frac{1}{4}(\alpha(\gamma'))^2ds.\]
    Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
	\[|[\alpha](\sigma)|=\left|\int_\gamma\alpha\right|=\left|\int_0^{L} \alpha(\gamma')ds\right|\le L_\sigma(t)^{1/2}(\int \alpha(\gamma')^2ds)^{1/2}.\]
    Because $\gamma$ is a stable closed geodesic, it follows that
    \[\int_{\gamma}R(\gamma(s))ds\le 0.\] Combining the above, we deduce that
	\[D_-L_\sigma(t)\ge \int_0^L-\frac{1}{2}R+\frac{1}{4}(\alpha(\gamma'))^2ds\ge \frac{[\alpha](\sigma)^2}{4}L_\sigma(t)^{-1}.\]
    Solving this differential inequality yields
	\[L_\sigma(t)^2\ge\frac{[\alpha](\sigma)^2}{2}t+L_\sigma(0)^2.\]
    In particular, $L_\sigma(t)$ is non-decreasing in $t$. Since $L(t)=\inf_{\sigma\neq0}L_\sigma(t)$, we conclude that $L(t)$ is also non-decreasing.

label: develop
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove (i), we apply
\cite[Proposition 11.5]{fukaya1990hausdorff} to see that $(X,d)$
can only be a circle, an interval, or a point.
By \cite[Theorem 4.1]{katz2020torus}, the interval case is ruled out.
The diameter estimate follows directly from
Gromov--Hausdorff convergence.

To prove (ii), we first establish a controlled contraction property
on the universal covers. Fix $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$.
We claim that 
for all sufficiently large $i$, every loop
$\gamma$ in $\tilde M_i$, based at a point $q$, admits a based
contraction $\{\gamma_s\}_{s\in[0,1]}$ satisfying $\gamma_0=\gamma$, $\gamma_1(t)=q$ for all $t\in [0,1]$ and
\begin{equation}\label{e:controlled.loop.contraction}
    L_{\tilde g_i}(\gamma_s)
    \le e^\epsilon L_{\tilde g_i}(\gamma)
    \qquad\text{for every }s\in[0,1].
\end{equation}

Suppose first that $X$ is a circle. By the \cite{cheeger1992nilpotent}, for sufficiently
large $i$ there is an invariant metric $h_i$ on the circle
fibration $M_i\to S^1$ satisfying $e^{-\epsilon}g_i\le h_i\le e^\epsilon g_i$.
After lifting to the universal cover, choosing arclength on the
lifted base, and removing the connection term, we obtain global
coordinates $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$ in which $\tilde h_i=dx^2+f_i(x)^2dy^2$.
Write $q=(x_0,y_0)$. First contract the $y$-coordinate of $\gamma$
linearly toward $y_0$, keeping its $x$-coordinate fixed. Then
contract the remaining $x$-coordinate linearly toward $x_0$.
Both stages fix $q$ and do not increase $\tilde h_i$-length.
Consequently,
\[
    L_{\tilde g_i}(\gamma_s)
    \le e^{\epsilon/2}L_{\tilde h_i}(\gamma_s)
    \le e^{\epsilon/2}L_{\tilde h_i}(\gamma)
    \le e^\epsilon L_{\tilde g_i}(\gamma),
\]
which proves \eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction}.

If $X$ is a point, let $d_i=\operatorname{diam}(M_i,g_i)\to0$
and normalize the metrics by $\hat g_i=d_i^{-2}g_i$.
Then
\[
    \operatorname{diam}(M_i,\hat g_i)=1,
    \qquad
    |\operatorname{Rm}(\hat g_i)|\le Kd_i^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
After passing to a subsequence, $(M_i,\hat g_i)\xrightarrow{GH}(S^1,d)$ or $(M_i,\hat g_i)\xrightarrow{C^{1,\alpha}}(\mathbb{T}^2,g_\infty)$.
In the former case, the preceding invariant-metric approximation
applies. In the latter case, $g_\infty$ is flat, so $\hat g_i$ is bilipschitz to a fixed flat metric $g_\infty$ for sufficiently
large $i$. Thus $\hat g_i$ satisfies \eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction}. Rescaling preserves the length ratio in
\eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction}, and thus the claim is proved.

We first use \eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction} to obtain a
uniform injectivity-radius bound. Choose $\delta>0$ such that $e^\epsilon\delta<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt K}$.
Suppose that $\operatorname{inj}_{\tilde g_i}(q)=r<\delta$
for some $q\in\tilde M_i$. The curvature bound implies that
there are no conjugate points at distance less than
$\pi/\sqrt K$. Thus Klingenberg's cut-locus lemma gives a
nonconstant geodesic loop based at $q$ of length $2r$.
By \eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction}, it contracts through
based loops of length at most $2e^\epsilon r<\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt K},$
contradicting Klingenberg's long homotopy lemma.
Hence $\operatorname{inj}_{\tilde g_i}(q)\ge\delta$
    for every $q\in\tilde M_i$.

The universal covers are therefore noncollapsing, and standard
pointed compactness gives, after passing to a subsequence, $(\tilde M_i,\tilde g_i,p_i)
    \xrightarrow{pt\  C^{1,\alpha}}(M_\infty,g_\infty,p_\infty)$.

By \eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction}, any loop in $M_\infty$
is approximated by loops in $\tilde M_i$ whose based contractions
remain in a uniformly bounded ball. Pulling these contractions
back through the convergence maps shows that the original loop
is null-homotopic. Hence $M_\infty$ is simply connected.

Minimizing geodesic rays in the universal covers pass to a ray
in $M_\infty$, so the limit is noncompact. Being also simply
connected, $M_\infty$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$.
This completes the proof.

label: c:convergence_CFG
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{alpha.norm.estimate} and Theorem~\ref{type.iii.estimate}, we have the estimates
\[
|\alpha_{s_i}(t)|_{g_{s_i}(t)}^2 \le \frac{c_0 s_i}{1 + \frac{c_0}{2} s_i t}, \qquad 
|R(g_{s_i}(t))| \le \frac{C s_i}{1+s_i t}.
\]
In particular, for any $T_0>0$, these yield uniform bounds on the curvature and on $|\alpha|$ over the time interval $[T_0,\infty)$. Therefore, the noncollapsing result in Theorem \ref{develop} and the compactness theorem in~\cite{guo2025alpha} apply and give the smooth pointed convergence on the universal cover.


    By Theorem~\ref{type.iii.estimate} and Gromov's compactness theorem \cite[Theorem 5.3]{gromov2007metric}, there exists a metric space $(X,d)$ such that $(M, g_{s_i}(1))\to (X,d)$ in the Gromov--Hausdorff topology. By Theorem~\ref{volume.estimate} and Theorem~\ref{develop}, we know that $(X,d)$ is either $(S^1, d)$ or a point $\{\mathrm{pt}\}$. The equivariant convergence and the fact that $G_\infty$ acts by isometries on $(\mathbb{R}^2,\tilde g_\infty(1))$ follow from \cite{fukaya1988boundary}.
Because $\tilde\alpha_{s_i}(1)$ is invariant under $G_i$, the equivariant smooth convergence on the universal cover implies that $\tilde \alpha_\infty(1)$ is invariant under $G_\infty$. 
    
    We would like to show that $G_\infty$ acts by isometries on $(\mathbb{R}^2,\tilde g_\infty(t))$ and preserves $\tilde\alpha_\infty(t)$ for any $t\in (0,\infty)$. Fix $\gamma_\infty\in G_\infty$. By equivariant convergence at
    time one, there exist $\gamma_i\in G_i$ converging locally uniformly
    to $\gamma_\infty$.
    Since the $\gamma_i$ are time-one isometries, their differentials
    are uniformly bounded on compact sets. The identity
    \[
    \gamma_i\circ\exp_p^{\tilde g_i(1)}
    =
    \exp_{\gamma_i(p)}^{\tilde g_i(1)}\circ d\gamma_i|_p
    \]
    and smooth convergence of the metrics upgrade this convergence
    to $C^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Passing to the limit in
    \[
    \gamma_i^*\tilde g_i(t)=\tilde g_i(t),
    \qquad
    \gamma_i^*\tilde\alpha_i(t)=\tilde\alpha_i(t)
    \]
    shows that $G_\infty$ preserves both $\tilde g_\infty(t)$ and
    $\tilde\alpha_\infty(t)$ for every $t>0$.
    
    We now show that $G_\infty$ is either $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$. For $\delta>0$ sufficiently small, consider the local fundamental group $\pi_1(M_i,x_i;\delta)$ of \cite[Definition 7.8]{fukaya1990hausdorff}. A globally null-homotopic based loop of length at most $2\delta$ lifts to a closed loop on $\tilde M_i$. By~\eqref{e:controlled.loop.contraction}, it contracts through based loops of length at most $2e^\epsilon\delta<4\delta$, so the projected contraction lies in $B(x_i,2\delta)$. Thus no globally trivial short loop remains locally nontrivial, and the local pseudogroup identifies with restrictions of the deck action of $\pi_1(M_i)$ on $\tilde M_i$. Let $H$ denote its limit pseudogroup.

    
    If $(X,d)=(S^1,d)$, then by \cite[Proposition 11.5]{fukaya1990hausdorff}, the action of $H$ is free since $X$ is a codimension one manifold. Because $G_\infty$ is locally isomorphic to $H$, the action of $G_\infty$ is free. Consequently, $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a principal $G_\infty$-bundle over $S^1$. A standard argument then shows $G_\infty \cong \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$.
    
    If $(X,d)=\{\mathrm{pt}\}$, $G_\infty$ is abelian because it is the limit of abelian groups. Furthermore, since $X$ is a point, $G_\infty$ acts transitively on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Choosing a basepoint $p\in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\mathbb{R}^2\cong G_\infty/K$, where $K \subset G_\infty$ is the isotropy subgroup at $p$. For any $x\in \mathbb{R}^2$, choose $g\in G_\infty$ such that $g\cdot p=x$. Then for any $k\in K$, we have $k\cdot x=k\cdot(g\cdot p)=g\cdot(k\cdot p)=g\cdot p=x$. Thus, $k$ acts trivially on $\mathbb{R}^2$. It follows that $K=\{e\}$ is trivial, and therefore $G_\infty\cong \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}$ as a Lie group.

body_md:
\label{invariant.alpha.ricci.flow}

label: W+.F.mu.nu.=0
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\bar \alpha(t)$ has no fiber component, $\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{W}_+\ge0$ follows from Theorem~\ref{t:evolution.of.w+.functional}.
    
    If $\mathcal{W}_+$ is constant, then by Theorem~\ref{t:evolution.of.w+.functional} we have 
    \begin{align}
        &F_{\mu\nu}^i=0,\label{W+.F.mu.nu.=0}\\
	    &g^{\mu\nu}G_{ij;\mu\nu}-g^{\mu\nu}G^{kl}G_{ik,\mu}G_{jl,\nu}-g^{\mu\nu}G_{ij,\mu}f_{,\nu}=0,\label{W+.Gij=0}\\
        &R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}a_\mu a_\nu-\frac{1}{4}G^{ij}G_{jk,\mu}G^{kl}G_{li,\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g^{\gamma\delta}G_{ij}F_{\mu\gamma}^iF_{\nu\delta}^j+f_{;\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2t}g_{\mu\nu}=0,\label{W+g.mu.nu.=0}\\
        &d_g^*a+i_{\nabla f}a=0.\label{W+d^*_fa=0}
	\end{align}
	Multiplying \eqref{W+.Gij=0} by $G^{ij}$ and summing over indices gives 
	\[\Delta\log \det (G_{ij})-\langle \nabla \log \det (G_{ij}),\nabla f\rangle=0.\]
	Integrating the left-hand side against $\log(\det (G_{ij}) )e^{-f}\, d\operatorname{vol}_B$ and applying the integration by parts formula, we get $\int_B|\nabla \log\det(G_{ij})|^2 e^{-f}\, d\operatorname{vol}_B=0$. Thus
    \begin{equation}\label{nabla.log.det.G=0}
	    G^{ij}G_{ij,\mu}=(\nabla\log\det (G_{ij}))_\mu=0.
	\end{equation} Hence $\det (G_{ij})$ is a constant in space. In particular
	\begin{equation}\label{Delta.log.det.G=0}
	    G^{ij}(g^{\mu\nu}G_{ij;\mu\nu}-g^{\mu\nu}G_{ik,\mu}G^{kl}G_{lj,\nu})=\Delta \log\det(G_{ij})=0.
	\end{equation}
    Plugging \eqref{W+.F.mu.nu.=0}, \eqref{W+d^*_fa=0}, \eqref{nabla.log.det.G=0} and \eqref{Delta.log.det.G=0} into \eqref{e:invariant.alpha.ricci.flow}, we have
    \begin{equation}\label{evolve.by.L.nabla.f}
        \frac{\partial G_{ij}}{\partial t}=g^{\mu\nu}G_{ij,\mu}f_{,\nu},\quad\frac{\partial A^i_\mu}{\partial t}=0,\quad \frac{\partial g_{\mu\nu}}{\partial t}=2f_{;\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{t}g_{\mu\nu},\quad\frac{\partial a_\mu}{\partial t}=(di_{\nabla f}a)_\mu.
    \end{equation}
	In particular
    $\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\log\det G_{ij}=G^{ij}\frac{\partial G_{ij}}{\partial t}=0$ by \eqref{nabla.log.det.G=0}. Hence $\det (G_{ij})$ is constant in spacetime. Moreover, from (\ref{evolve.by.L.nabla.f}) the flow evolves by a diffeomorphism generated by $\nabla f$ and a scaling of $g_{\mu\nu}$. Thus we have
	\[\frac{\partial \bar R^{\bar \alpha}}{\partial t}=\langle\nabla f,\nabla \bar R^{\bar \alpha}\rangle-\frac{\bar R^{\bar \alpha}}{t}.\]
Since $F=0$, $b=0$, and $\det G$ is spatially constant,
$\bar R_{i\mu}=0$,
$\bar\Delta\bar R^{\bar\alpha}
=\Delta\bar R^{\bar\alpha}$, and
$d_{\bar g}^*\bar\alpha=d_g^*a$.
The evolution equation consequently gives
\[
\frac{\partial\bar R^{\bar\alpha}}{\partial t}
=
\Delta\bar R^{\bar\alpha}
+2|\bar R_{ij}|^2
+2\left|\bar R_{\mu\nu}-\frac14a_\mu a_\nu\right|^2
+\frac12(d_g^*a)^2.
\]
Combining this with
\[
\frac{\partial\bar R^{\bar\alpha}}{\partial t}
=
\langle\nabla f,\nabla\bar R^{\bar\alpha}\rangle
-\frac{\bar R^{\bar\alpha}}{t}
\]
and completing the square yields
\begin{equation}\label{equation.for.R.alpha+n/2t}
\begin{aligned}
&\Delta\left(\bar R^{\bar\alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}\right)
+2|\bar R_{ij}|^2
+2\left|\bar R_{\mu\nu}-\frac14a_\mu a_\nu
+\frac{1}{2t}g_{\mu\nu}\right|^2\\
&\qquad
+\frac12(d_g^*a)^2
-\frac1t\left(\bar R^{\bar\alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}\right)
=
\left\langle\nabla f,
\nabla\left(\bar R^{\bar\alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}\right)
\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
At a negative minimum of
$\bar R^{\bar\alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}$, the left-hand side
would be strictly positive while the right-hand side vanishes.
Thus we must have $\min_B \bar R^{\bar \alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}\ge 0$.
	
    On the other hand, plugging (\ref{W+.F.mu.nu.=0}) and (\ref{Delta.log.det.G=0}) into \cite[(4.6),(4.7)]{lott2007long}, we have 
    \begin{align*}
        \bar R_{ij}=&-\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}G_{ij;\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}G^{kl}G_{ik,\mu}G_{jl,\nu},\quad\bar R_{i\mu}=0,\\
	\bar R_{\mu\nu}=&R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}G^{ij}G_{jk,\mu}G^{kl}G_{il,\nu},\\
	\bar R=&R-\frac{1}{4}g^{\mu\nu}G^{ij}G_{jk,\mu}G^{kl}G_{il,\nu}.
    \end{align*}
	Tracing (\ref{W+g.mu.nu.=0}) by $g^{\mu\nu}$, we get 
    \begin{equation}\label{R.mu.f=0}
	    \bar R^{\bar \alpha}+\Delta f+\frac{n}{2t}=R-\frac{1}{4}|a|^2-\frac{1}{4}g^{\mu\nu}G^{ij}G_{jk,\mu}G^{kl}G_{il,\nu}+\Delta f+\frac{n}{2t}=0.
	\end{equation}
	Then by the divergence theorem, we have \[\int_B (\bar R^{\bar \alpha} +\frac{n}{2t})\, d\operatorname{vol}_B=-\int_B\Delta f\, d\operatorname{vol}_B=0.\]
	Since $\min_B\bar R^{\bar \alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}\ge0$, we have $\bar R^{\bar \alpha}+\frac{n}{2t}\equiv0$. Hence, by (\ref{R.mu.f=0}) and the fact that $B$ is closed, we conclude that $f$ is a constant. Due to (\ref{evolve.by.L.nabla.f}), we have (iii). By \eqref{W+d^*_fa=0}, we have (v). By (\ref{equation.for.R.alpha+n/2t}), we have $\bar R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}a_\mu a_\nu+\frac{1}{2t}g_{\mu\nu}=\bar R_{ij}=0$ which gives the equations in (iv).

\]
if there are:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item A sequence of open subsets $\{U_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ of $B_\infty$, each containing $p_\infty$, such that any compact subset of $B_\infty$ eventually lies in all $U_j$, and
    
    \item Open subsets $V_{i,j} \subset B_i$ containing $p_i$ and isomorphisms
    \[
    \phi_{i,j} : \pi_\infty^{-1}(U_j) \to \pi_i^{-1}(V_{i,j})
    \]
    sending $\pi_\infty^{-1}(p_\infty)$ to $\pi_i^{-1}(p_i)$, such that
    
    \item For all $j$,
    \[
    \lim_{i \to \infty} \phi_{i,j}^* g_i(t) = g_\infty(t),\lim_{i \to \infty} \phi_{i,j}^* \alpha_i(t) = \alpha_\infty(t)
    \]
    smoothly on $\pi_\infty^{-1}(U_j) \times \left[ j^{-1},\,  j\right]$.
\end{enumerate}

    (v) The $1$-form $\hat a$ is harmonic on $\hat B$:
\[
d\hat a=0,\qquad d_{\hat g}^*\hat a=0.
\]

label: e:u_equation
title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{c:conditional.monotonicity}, it suffices to construct a solution to \eqref{e:f_equation} along $(\hat g(t), \hat \alpha(t))$ on $(0,\infty)$ for which $\mathcal{W}_+$ remains constant. We follow similar ideas in \cite[Proposition 4.39]{lott2010dimensional}.

We write $u=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-f}$. Then \eqref{e:f_equation} is equivalent to 
\begin{equation}\label{e:u_equation}
    \left(\frac{\partial }{\partial t}+\Delta-R+\frac{1}{4}g^{\mu\nu}G^{ij}G_{jk,\mu}G^{kl}G_{il,\nu}+\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}g^{\gamma\delta}G_{ij}F_{\mu\gamma}^iF_{\nu\delta}^j+\frac{1}{4}g^{\mu\nu}a_\mu a_\nu\right)u=0.
\end{equation}
Note that if $u$ is a solution to \eqref{e:u_equation}, then $\int_B u  \,d\operatorname{vol}_B$ is constant in $t$. Choose $\delta_j\downarrow0$ and $t_j\uparrow\infty$ with $\delta_j<t_j$, so that $[\delta_j,t_j]$ exhausts $(0,\infty)$. Let $\tilde{u}_j(t)$ be a solution to \eqref{e:u_equation} on the interval $[\delta_j,t_j]$ with terminal condition
\[
\tilde{u}_j(t_j) = \frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}(B, g_{\mu\nu}(t_j))}.
\]
For any $0<\delta<T$, we claim that a subsequence of the $\tilde{u}_j$'s converges smoothly on the time interval $[\delta,T]$.

To see this, at time $T+1$ we know that if $\delta_j<\delta$ and $t_j\ge T+1$ then $\tilde{u}_j(T+1) \ge 0$ and
\[
\int_B \tilde{u}_j(T+1)\, d\operatorname{vol}_B = 1.
\]
Solving the conjugate heat equation with terminal data at time $T+1$, and restricting the solution to the time interval $[\delta,T]$, gives a smoothing operator from the space of terminal data
\[
\left\{ \tilde{u} \in L^1(B) : \tilde{u} \ge 0,\ \int_B \tilde{u}\, d\operatorname{vol}_B(T+1) = 1 \right\}
\]
to $C^\infty([\delta,T]\times B)$ by the heat kernel estimate \cite{chau2011pseudolocality}. Thus we have the derivative bounds needed to extract a subsequence of the $\tilde{u}_j$'s that converges smoothly on $[\delta,T]$. By a diagonal argument over $[1/k,k]$, $k\ge2$, we can extract a subsequence of the $\tilde{u}_j$'s that converges smoothly on compact subsets of $(0,\infty)$ to a nonzero solution $\bar{u}(t)$ of \eqref{e:u_equation}, defined for $t \in (0,\infty)$.

One can show, as in \cite[Proof of Proposition 7.5]{kleiner2008notes}, that $\bar{u}(t) > 0$. If $\bar f(t)$ is given by
\[
\bar u(t) = (4\pi t)^{-n/2} e^{-\bar{f}(t)},
\]
then $\mathcal{W}_+(\bar G_{ij},\bar A^i_\mu,\bar g_{\mu\nu},\bar a_\mu,0,\bar f,t)$ is non-decreasing in $t$. We write
\[
\mathcal{W}_{+,\infty} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathcal{W}_+(\bar G_{ij}(t), \bar A^i_{\mu}(t), \bar g_{\mu\nu}(t),\bar a_\mu(t),0, \bar f(t),t),
\]
if we are in the case $s_i\to\infty$ and 
\[
\mathcal{W}_{+,\infty} = \lim_{t \to0} \mathcal{W}_+(\bar G_{ij}(t), \bar A^i_{\mu}(t), \bar g_{\mu\nu}(t),\bar a_\mu(t),0, \bar f(t),t),
\]
if we are in the case $s_i\to0$.
Note that $\mathcal{W}_{+,\infty}$ is possibly $\pm\infty$ for the moment.

Next, we put 
$(\bar g_{s_i}(t),\bar \alpha_{s_i}(t))=(s_i^{-1}\bar G_{ij}(s_i t),\bar A_\mu^i(s_i t),s_i^{-1}\bar g_{\mu\nu}(s_i t),\bar a_\mu(s_i t),0)$ and $u_i(t) = s_i^{n/2}\bar{u}(s_it)$. By assumption, $\lim_{i \to \infty} (\bar g_{s_i}(t),\bar\alpha_{s_i}(t)) = (\hat g(t),\hat\alpha(t))$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:convergence.invariant.alpha.RF}. Then by the same smoothing argument as above, there is a subsequence of $\{u_i(t)\}_{i=1}^\infty$ that converges smoothly on compact subsets of $(0,\infty)$ to a solution $\hat u(t)$ on $\hat B$. Define $\hat f(t)$ by
\[
\hat u(t) = (4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-\hat f(t)}.
\]
Then after passing to a subsequence of $s_i$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\mathcal{W}_+(\hat G_{ij}(t), \hat A^i_{\mu}(t), \hat g_{\mu\nu}(t),\hat a_\mu(t),0, \hat f(t),t)\\
=& \lim_{i \to \infty} \mathcal{W}_+(s_i^{-1}\bar G_{ij}(s_i t),\bar A_\mu^i(s_i t),s_i^{-1}\bar g_{\mu\nu}(s_i t),\bar a_\mu(s_i t),0,\bar f(s_i t),t) \\
=& \lim_{i \to \infty} \mathcal{W}_+(\bar G_{ij}(s_i t),\bar A_\mu^i(s_i t),\bar g_{\mu\nu}(s_i t),\bar a_\mu(s_i t),0,\bar f(s_i t),s_it) \\
=& \mathcal{W}_{+,\infty}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This shows that $\mathcal{W}_{+,\infty}< \infty$ and that
\[
\mathcal{W}_+(\hat G_{ij}(t), \hat A^i_{\mu}(t), \hat g_{\mu\nu}(t),\hat a_\mu(t),0, \hat f(t),t)
\]
is constant in $t$. This finishes the proof.

label: 1d.alpha.expander
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{1d.alpha.expander}
Let $(\bar g(t),\bar\alpha(t))$ be a locally $\mathbb{R}^N$-invariant $\alpha$-Ricci flow on $S^1$, defined for $t\in(0,\infty)$, with trivial linear holonomy and no fiber component. Let $s_i\to0$ or $s_i\to\infty$. After time-independent identifications of the bases and constant linear changes of the fiber coordinates, write
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_i(t):=s_i^{-1}\bar g(s_it)
&=u_i(t)(dx^0)^2+(G_i)_{jk}(t)(dx^j+A_i^j(t))(dx^k+A_i^k(t)),\\
\alpha_i(t):=\bar\alpha(s_it)&=a_i(t)\,dx^0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Suppose that $\hat G>0$, $\hat u>0$, and
\[
(G_i,u_i,a_i)\longrightarrow(\hat G,\hat u,\hat a)
\quad\text{in }C^\infty(S^1\times[\delta,T]),
\qquad 0<\delta<T<\infty.
\]
Then, choosing $x^0$ to be arclength at time one, a constant linear change of the fiber coordinates, and an orientation of $S^1$, we have
\[
\hat G_{ij}=\delta_{ij},\qquad \hat u(t)=t,\qquad \hat a=\sqrt2.
\]
In particular, for any time-independent flat connection $\hat A$, the metric and $1$-form determined by $(\hat G,\hat A,\hat u,\hat a,0)$ lift to a flow isometric to $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ on the universal cover.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\dim B=1$ and $b=0$, we have $F=0$, and the equations for $G,u,a$, equation~\eqref{e:f_equation}, and $\mathcal{W}_+$ are independent of $A$. Moreover, $\mathcal{W}_+$ is unchanged by constant linear changes of the fiber coordinates. Thus the conjugate heat construction and passage to the limit in the proof of Corollary~\ref{alpha.expander} apply to the assumed convergence of $(G_i,u_i,a_i)$: the limiting $\mathcal{W}_+$ is constant, and we obtain~\eqref{alpha.expander.G.ij},~\eqref{alpha.expander.R.mu.nu}, $\partial_t\hat G=\partial_t\hat a=0$, and $\hat u(t)=t\hat u(1)$. Choose $x^0$ to be arclength at time one, so that $\hat u(t)=t$. By triviality of the linear holonomy, $\hat G_{ij}$ and $\hat a$ are periodic functions of $x^0$.
    Then equation (\ref{alpha.expander.G.ij}) becomes
    \[\hat G_{ij}''-\hat G^{kl}\hat G_{ik}'\hat G_{jl}'=0\] where $'=\partial_{0}$.
    In other words, $(\hat G^{-1}\hat G')'=0$. Thus $\hat G^{-1}\hat G'=X$ for some constant matrix $X$. Integrating $\hat G'=\hat GX$, we get $\hat G(x^0)=\hat G(0)\exp(x^0X)$. We can choose coordinates such that $\hat G(0)=I$. Then $\hat G'(0)=X$ is symmetric and in particular, $X$ is diagonalizable and has real eigenvalues. Since $\hat G$ is periodic in $x^0$, we must have $X=0$ and hence $\hat G=I$.
    Equation (\ref{alpha.expander.R.mu.nu}) now reads
	\[
		-\frac{1}{4}\hat a^2+\frac{1}{2}=0.
	\]
	Hence adjusting the orientation of $S^1$ if necessary, we have $\hat a=\sqrt 2$.
Finally, on the universal cover, write $\hat A^i=d\psi^i$; the time-independent change $y^i=x^i+\psi^i$ removes $\hat A$ and gives the asserted isometry.

label: r:connection.convergence
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{r:connection.convergence}
Corollary~\ref{1d.alpha.expander} does not require $A_i\to\hat A$. Even though $F_i=0$, normalization of the fiber coordinates may make $A_i$ unbounded, so convergence of $(G_i,u_i,a_i)$ need not imply convergence in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:convergence.invariant.alpha.RF}. In the groupoid setting, different flat connections with the same $G$ and base metric give equivalent Riemannian groupoids by~\cite[Lemma~5.11]{lott2010dimensional}, although the global bundle metrics need not be isometric. To avoid groupoid language, we use convergence of $(G_i,u_i,a_i)$ directly; since $F=b=0$, these are precisely the coefficients needed in the entropy argument.

label: tuple.equivalence
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{tuple.equivalence}
The equivalence class $[\mathbf{\bar g}]$ consists of the tuples
\[
\left(
S^T( G\circ\phi)S,\,
( u\circ\phi)(\phi')^2,\,
\eta\circ\phi+\sqrt2(\phi-x^0)-c
\right),
\]
where $S\in\operatorname{GL}(N,\mathbb{R})$, $c\in\mathbb{R}$, and $\phi$ is a smooth orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^1$. In the expression $\phi-x^0$, we use a degree-one lift of $\phi$ to $\mathbb{R}$, denoted by the same symbol, satisfying $\phi(x^0+\ell)=\phi(x^0)+\ell$. Thus $\phi-x^0$ is $\ell$-periodic and defines a real-valued function on $S^1$. Changing the lift adds an integer multiple of $\ell$, which is absorbed into the constant $c$. The change in $\eta$ is obtained by
\[
\phi^*\bar\alpha
=\sqrt 2d\phi+d(\eta\circ\phi)=\left(\sqrt2+\partial_0\bigl(\eta\circ\phi
+\sqrt2(\phi-x^0)-c\bigr)\right)dx^0.
\]
For a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ and nonintegral $r>0$, let $h^r(S^1;V)$ be the closure of $C^\infty(S^1;V)$ in $C^r(S^1;V)$, with the inherited norm. Set $\mathbb V=\operatorname{Sym}_N\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$, where $\operatorname{Sym}_N$ is the space of real symmetric $N\times N$ matrices. For nonintegral $r>1$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:distance.to.expander.class}
 d_r([\mathbf{\bar g}],[\mathbf g^*])
 =\inf_{\mathbf v\in[\mathbf{\bar g}]}
 \|\mathbf v-\mathbf g^*\|_{h^r(S^1;\mathbb V)}.
\end{equation}
Fix $0<\rho<\theta<1$. For $\delta,\epsilon>0$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal V_\delta
&=\{[\mathbf{\bar g}]:d_{1+\theta}([\mathbf{\bar g}],[\mathbf g^*])<\delta\},\\
\mathcal U_\epsilon
&=\{[\mathbf{\bar g}]:d_{1+\rho}([\mathbf{\bar g}],[\mathbf g^*])<\epsilon\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
We have
\[
d_r([\mathbf{\bar g}],[\mathbf g^*])=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
[\mathbf{\bar g}]=[\mathbf g^*].
\]
Indeed, suppose that representatives corresponding to $(S_j,\phi_j,c_j)$ converge to $(I,1,0)$ in $h^r$. Since $G>0$ and $u>0$, this convergence implies that $S_j$ and $S_j^{-1}$ are bounded and $0<c\le\phi_j'\le C$ for constants independent of $j$. After normalizing the degree-one lifts by $\phi_j(0)\in[0,\ell]$ and passing to a subsequence, $S_j\to S\in\operatorname{GL}(N,\mathbb{R})$ and $\phi_j\to\phi$ in $C^1$, where $\phi$ is a smooth orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism. Since each $\phi_j$ is onto, convergence of the first component gives $S^T G S=I$ at every point. Write $ a=\sqrt2+\partial_0\eta$. Convergence of the second and third components gives $ a>0$ and
\[
\left(\frac{ a^2}{ u}\right)\circ\phi=2,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 u=\frac12 a^2.
\]
Thus $y=x^0+\eta(x^0)/\sqrt2$ defines an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^1$, in which $\bar\alpha=\sqrt2\,dy$ and the base metric is $dy^2$. Together with the constant fiber change $S$, this gives the tuple $(I,1,0)$ after choosing the additive constant. The converse follows directly from~\eqref{eq:distance.to.expander.class}. In particular,
\[
\bigcap_{\epsilon>0}\mathcal U_\epsilon=\{[\mathbf g^*]\}.
\]

label: type.3.estimates.blow.down
title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{c:convergence_CFG}, the limit is $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$-invariant and descends to an $\mathbb{R}$-invariant flow $(\bar g(t),\bar\alpha(t))$ over $B=S^1$. Write its coefficients as $G,u,a$, with base metric $u(t)d\theta^2$ and $\bar\alpha(t)=a(t)d\theta$. By Theorems~\ref{diameter.bound},~\ref{alpha.norm.estimate}, and~\ref{type.iii.estimate},
\begin{equation}\label{type.3.estimates.blow.down}
\operatorname{diam}(B,u(t)d\theta^2)\le C\sqrt t,\qquad
|R(\bar g(t))|\le \frac Ct,\qquad
|\bar\alpha(t)|^2\le \frac2t.
\end{equation}
As in the proof of Corollary~\ref{alpha.expander}, construct a normalized solution of~\eqref{e:f_equation} on compact positive-time intervals and pass to a diagonal limit on $(0,\infty)$. Lemma~\ref{volume.ratio.lower.bound.by.W_+} and Corollary~\ref{c:conditional.monotonicity} give
\[
\frac12\log(4\pi)-\log\bigl(t^{-1/2}\operatorname{vol}(B,u(t)d\theta^2)\bigr)
\le\mathcal{W}_+(t)\le\mathcal{W}_+(1),\qquad 0<t\le1.
\]
Consequently, by~\eqref{type.3.estimates.blow.down},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base.length.backward.bounds}
0<c\le t^{-1/2}\operatorname{vol}(B,u(t)d\theta^2)
=2t^{-1/2}\operatorname{diam}(B,u(t)d\theta^2)\le C,
\qquad 0<t\le1.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\mathcal{W}_+$ is bounded from below on $(0,1]$.

Let $t_i\to0$ and write $(g_i(t),\alpha_i(t))=(t_i^{-1}\bar g(t_it),\bar\alpha(t_it))$. By \eqref{eq:base.length.backward.bounds} we choose base arclength $\theta\in\mathbb{R}/\ell_i\mathbb{Z}$ and normalize the fiber coordinate so that
\[
g_i(1)=d\theta^2+G_i(\theta)(dv+A_i(\theta)d\theta)^2,
\qquad \alpha_i(1)=a_i(\theta)d\theta,
\qquad G_i(0)=1,\qquad c\le\ell_i\le C.
\]
These base identifications and fiber normalizations are fixed in time; in the following time-one estimates, we write $G_i=G_i(1)$ and $a_i=a_i(1)$.
We have
\begin{equation}\label{scalar.in.terms.of.Gi}
    R_i:=R(g_i(1))=
-(\log G_i)''-\frac12((\log G_i)')^2.
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{type.3.estimates.blow.down}, $|R(g_i(1))|\le C$. Evaluating \eqref{scalar.in.terms.of.Gi} at minimum and maximum of the periodic function $(\log G_i)'$ and integrating from $\theta=0$ gives
\[
| (\log G_i)' |\le2\sqrt C,
\qquad C_1^{-1}\le G_i\le C_1.
\]
The smoothing estimates in~\cite{guo2025alpha}, used in Corollary~\ref{c:convergence_CFG}, give bounds on all covariant derivatives of $R_i$ and $\alpha_i$ on bounded lifted balls. Locally choose the fiber coordinate so that $A_i=0$. Since $\theta$ is base arclength, $\partial_\theta$ is then a unit vector field with $\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_\theta=0$. By \eqref{eq:base.length.backward.bounds}, we have
\[
|\partial_\theta^k R_i|\le C_k,\qquad
|a_i|=|\alpha_i|\le\sqrt2,\qquad
\partial_\theta^k a_i
=(\nabla^k\alpha_i)(\partial_\theta,\ldots,\partial_\theta),
\qquad |\partial_\theta^k a_i|\le C_k.
\]
The identity
\[
G_i''=\frac{(G_i')^2}{2G_i}-R_iG_i
\]
then bounds every derivative of $G_i$ inductively. After parametrizing the bases with a common period $\ell$, the base coefficient at time one is $u_i(1)=(\ell_i/\ell)^2$. Together with these time-one bounds, the metric distortion bounds from~\eqref{type.3.estimates.blow.down}, equations~\eqref{e:invariant.alpha.ricci.flow}, and the positive-time smoothing estimates in~\cite{guo2025alpha} give, after passing to a diagonal subsequence with $\ell_i\to\ell_\infty>0$,
\[
(G_i(t),u_i(t),a_i(t))\longrightarrow(G_\infty(t),u_\infty(t),a_\infty(t))
\quad\text{in }C^\infty(S^1\times[\delta,T]),
\qquad 0<\delta<T<\infty.
\]

By Corollary~\ref{1d.alpha.expander}, we can choose coordinates so that $G_\infty(t)=1$, $u_\infty(t)=t$ and $a_\infty(t)=\sqrt2$. At time one, $(G_i(1),u_i(1),a_i(1))\longrightarrow(1,1,\sqrt2)$ in $C^\infty(S^1)$. Since $\bar\alpha$ evolves by an exact form, and $\alpha_i(1)=\bar\alpha(t_i)$, we can write $\eta_i'=a_i(1)-\sqrt2$ where $\eta_i\in C^\infty(S^1)$ satisfies $\int_0^\ell\eta_i\,d\theta=0$. Then we have $(G_i(1),u_i(1),\eta_i)\longrightarrow(1,1,0)$ in $h^{1+\theta}(S^1)$.
For $s>0$, write the blow-down tuple as
\[
\mathbf{\bar g}_s(t)
=\bigl(s^{-1}G(st),s^{-1}u(st),\eta(st)\bigr),
\qquad a=\sqrt2+\partial_0\eta.
\]
The constant fiber change $S=\sqrt s\,I$ gives
\[
[\mathbf{\bar g}_s(1)]=[(G(s),s^{-1}u(s),\eta(s))].
\] Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\delta(\epsilon)>0$ from Corollary~\ref{neighborhood.around.expander}. The preceding convergence implies $[\mathbf{\bar g}_{t_i}(1)]\in\mathcal V_\delta$ for all sufficiently large $i$. Fix $T>0$. Since $t_i\to0$, we have $T/t_i\ge1$ for all sufficiently large $i$. The blow-down by $t_i$, followed by the blow-down by $T/t_i$, is the blow-down by $T$. Therefore Corollary~\ref{neighborhood.around.expander} gives
\[
[\mathbf{\bar g}_T(1)]
=[(\mathbf{\bar g}_{t_i})_{T/t_i}(1)]
\in\mathcal U_\epsilon.
\]
Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ gives $[\mathbf{\bar g}_T(1)]=[\mathbf g^*]$ for every $T>0$.
Hence, in the original coordinates,
\[
G'=0,\qquad u(t)=\frac t2a(t)^2.
\]
Substituting into~\eqref{gauged.invariant.alpha.ricci.flow} gives
\[
\partial_t G=\partial_t a=\partial_t A=0.
\]
Thus, on the universal cover, $(\bar g(t),\bar\alpha(t))$ is isometric to $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$.

label: l:collapsing.generators
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:collapsing.generators}
    Suppose there exists a sequence $s_i\to\infty$ such that $(M,g_{s_i}(1))\xrightarrow{GH} (S^1,d)$. Then there are closed curves $\gamma_i,\sigma_i$ such that $[\gamma_i],[\sigma_i]$ generate $\pi_1(M)$ and $L(\gamma_i,g_{s_i}(1))\to0$ and $L(\sigma_i,g_{s_i}(1))\to L(S^1,d)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By \cite[Theorem 2.6]{cheeger1992nilpotent}, for some sequence $\epsilon_i\to0$, there exists an $\epsilon_i$-almost Riemannian submersion $F_i:(M,g_{s_i}(1))\to (S^1,d)$ such that $\operatorname{diam} F_i^{-1}(\theta)\le \epsilon_i$ for any $\theta\in S^1$.  Let $\gamma_i=F_i^{-1}(\theta)\cong S^1$ be one of the fibers of $F_i$. Then $L(\gamma_i,g_{s_i}(1))\to0$. Let $\sigma_{1,i}$ be the integral curve of the horizontal distribution of $F_i:M\to S^1$ such that $\sigma_{1,i}(0)=x\in M$ and $\sigma_{1,i}(1)\in F_i^{-1}(F_i(x))$. Let $\sigma_{2,i}$ be a shortest curve in $F_i^{-1}(F_i(x))$ connecting $\sigma_{1,i}(1)$ and $x$. Let $\sigma_i=\sigma_{1,i}\cup \sigma_{2,i}$. Then by \cite[Theorem 2.6]{cheeger1992nilpotent}, we have $L(\sigma_i,g_{s_i}(1))\le (1+\epsilon_i)L(S^1,d)+\epsilon_i$.  Since $M=\mathbb{T}^2$ is orientable, $F_i$ is a trivial fibration. Since $F_{i*}[\sigma_i]=[S^1]$, we have $[\gamma_i],[\sigma_i]$ generate $\pi_1(M)$.

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose for contradiction that there exists a sequence of indices $i \to \infty$ such that $[\alpha](\gamma_i)\neq0$. Then Theorem~\ref{growth.of.length.of.shortest.curve} applied to the flow $(g(t),\alpha(t))$ gives $L_{[\gamma_i]}(t)^2\ge\frac{1}{2}[\alpha](\gamma_i)^2 t+L_{[\gamma_i]}(0)^2$. In particular, $L(F_{i}^{-1}(\theta),g_{s_i}(1))\ge s_i^{-1/2}L_{[\gamma_i]}(s_i)\ge \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}|[\alpha](\gamma_i)|>0$. By Lemma~\ref{l:collapsing.generators}, we have $L(F_{i}^{-1}(\theta),g_{s_i}(1))\to0$, forcing $|[\alpha](\gamma_i)| \to 0$. By Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets}, since $[\alpha]$ is rational, if $|[\alpha](\gamma_i)|<\ell([\alpha])$, then $[\alpha](\gamma_i)=0$. This contradicts $[\alpha](\gamma_i)\neq0$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{no_fiber_component} 
Suppose $[\alpha]$ is rational and there is a sequence $s_i\to\infty$ such that $(M,g_{s_i}(1))\allowbreak\xrightarrow{GH} (S^1,d)$ and $(\tilde{g}_{s_i}(t), \tilde{\alpha}_{s_i}(t))\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(\tilde g_\infty(t), \tilde \alpha_\infty(t))$. head: environment
name: No fiber component

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that the limit has a nonzero fiber component. Then, by Corollary~\ref{fiber.constant.in.spacetime}, $\tilde{\alpha}_\infty(\partial_v)(\theta, v, t) = b \neq 0$ for any $(\theta, v, t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \times (0,\infty)$.

By \cite[Theorem 2.6]{cheeger1992nilpotent}, for $i$ sufficiently large, we have a smooth fibration map $F_i: (M, g_{s_i}(1)) \to (S^1, d)$ which is an $\epsilon_i$-almost Riemannian submersion. Since $M = \mathbb{T}^2$ is orientable and $F_i: M \to S^1$ is a fibration with fiber $S^1$, the fibration $F_i$ must be trivial.

Choose $0<\delta < \operatorname{inj}(S^1,d)$ sufficiently small. By the controlled-contraction argument in the proof of Corollary~\ref{c:convergence_CFG}, globally trivial short loops contract in the $2\delta$-ball, so the local fundamental group $\pi_1(M,x_i;\delta)$ identifies with restrictions of the deck action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\tilde M$. Let $\gamma_i$ be the fiber of $F_i$ as in Lemma~\ref{l:collapsing.generators} and \ref{l:zero.pairing.with.fiber}. Then, by the same argument as in \cite[Proposition 11.5]{fukaya1990hausdorff}, there exists $n_i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $0 < \lim_{i\to\infty} d\big([\gamma_i]^{n_i}(p), p\big) \le \delta$ for $p \in \tilde{M}$.

After passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $[\gamma_i]^{n_i} \to \gamma_\delta \in G_\infty$. Consequently, we have $0 < d(\gamma_\delta(p), p) \le \delta$. Since $\delta < \operatorname{inj}(S^1,d)$, $\gamma_\delta$ must be a translation purely in the $\partial_v$ direction.

Normalize and orient $v$ so that the metric on the fiber through $p$ at time one is $dv^2$ and $\gamma_\delta$ translates in the positive direction. Let $h>0$ be the intrinsic distance on this fiber from $p$ to $\gamma_\delta(p)$. Let $\eta_1$ be the curve along the $\mathbb{R}$-orbit from $p$ to $\gamma_\delta(p)$, and let $\eta_2$ be the shortest geodesic with respect to $\tilde{g}_\infty(1)$ from $\gamma_\delta(p)$ to $[\gamma_i]^{n_i}(p)$. Defining $\eta=\eta_1\cup\eta_2$, we have
\begin{align*}
        n_i[\alpha](\gamma_i) &= \int_{\pi(\eta)} \alpha_{s_i} = \int_{\eta} \tilde{\alpha}_{s_i} = \int_{\eta} \tilde{\alpha}_\infty + o(1) \\
        &= \int_{\eta_1} \tilde{\alpha}_\infty + \int_{\eta_2} \tilde{\alpha}_\infty + o(1) \\
        &= bh + \mathcal{E}_i,
    \end{align*}
where the error term $\mathcal{E}_i$ is bounded by
    \[
        |\mathcal{E}_i| \le \sup_{\mathbb{R}^2}|\tilde{\alpha}_\infty|_{\tilde{g}_\infty} d\big(\gamma_\delta(p), [\gamma_i]^{n_i}(p)\big) + o(1).
    \]Since $d\big(\gamma_\delta(p), [\gamma_i]^{n_i}(p)\big) \to 0$ as $i \to \infty$, the error term $\mathcal{E}_i$ vanishes in the limit. Thus, for $i$ sufficiently large, $[\alpha](\gamma_i) \neq 0$. This contradicts Lemma~\ref{l:zero.pairing.with.fiber}.

label: l:bounded.generator
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:bounded.generator}
Suppose
\[
(\tilde g_s(t),\tilde\alpha_s(t))
\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))
\quad\text{as }s\to\infty.
\]
Identify $\pi_1(M)$ with the group of deck transformations of the
universal cover and fix a basepoint $0\in\tilde M$. For every $L>0$,
there exist $s_0=s_0(L)>0$ and $L'=\sqrt 8 L>0$ such that for every
$s_1\ge s_0$ and $\gamma\in\pi_1(M)$ satisfying
\[
d_{\tilde g_{s_1}(1)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)\leq L
\]
we have
\[
\sup_{s\geq s_1}d_{\tilde g_s(1)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)\leq L'.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varepsilon\in (0,\frac{1}{3})$ and $R>1$, to be chosen below. By smooth convergence, there exists $s_0=s_0(\varepsilon,R)>0$ such that $(\tilde g_s(t),\tilde\alpha_s(t))$ are $\varepsilon$-close to $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ for any
$s\geq s_0$ on $B_R(g^*(1))\times [R^{-1},R]$. We use the
coordinates $(\theta,v)$ from \eqref{eq:flat_expander_model}.
Write
\[
D_s(\gamma)=d_{\tilde g_s(1)}(\gamma(0),0).
\]For any $\gamma$ satisfying $D_{s_1}(\gamma)\le L$, Theorem \ref{alpha.norm.estimate} gives
\[
|[\alpha](\gamma)|
\le \|\alpha_{s_1}(1)\|_{L^\infty(g_{s_1}(1))}L
\le \sqrt{2}L.
\]

Let $s\geq s_1$ be such that $D_s(\gamma)^2<(1-\varepsilon)R^2$.  We  
write $\gamma(0)=(\theta_0,v_0)$. Then $(v_0^2+\theta_0^2)\le (1-\varepsilon)^{-1}D_s(\gamma)^2< R^2$ and thus $(\theta_0,v_0)\in B_R(g^*(1))$.
Metric comparison
at times $1$ and $1\le r\le R$ gives
\begin{align}
d_{\tilde g_s(1)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)^2
&\geq (1-\varepsilon)(v_0^2+\theta_0^2),
\label{eq:estimate.g_s(1)}\\
d_{\tilde g_s(r)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)^2
&\leq (1+\varepsilon)(v_0^2+r\theta_0^2).
\label{eq:estimate.g_s(R)}
\end{align}

Because $\tilde\alpha_s(t)$ and $\alpha^*$ are closed, their integrals
depend only on the homotopy class. Integrating along the straight segment
from $0$ to $\gamma(0)$ therefore yields
\[
\left|[\alpha](\gamma)-\sqrt{2}\,\theta_0\right|
\leq \varepsilon\sqrt{v_0^2+\theta_0^2},
\]
where $[\alpha](\gamma)=\int_\gamma\tilde\alpha_s(t)$ is independent of
$s$ and $t$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:theta}
\theta_0^2
\leq [\alpha](\gamma)^2
+\varepsilon(v_0^2+\theta_0^2)\le 2L^2+\varepsilon(v_0^2+\theta_0^2).
\end{equation}
The scaling identity $\tilde g_{sR}(1)=R^{-1}\tilde g_s(R)$, together
with \eqref{eq:estimate.g_s(1)}--\eqref{eq:theta}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dg_sR(1)}
\begin{aligned}
    d_{\tilde g_{sR}(1)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)^2
\le& (1+\varepsilon)(\frac{v_0^2}{R}+\theta_0^2)\\
\le&(1+\varepsilon) (\frac{d_{\tilde g_s(1)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)^2}{(1-\varepsilon)R}+2L^2+\varepsilon(v_0^2+\theta_0^2))\\
\le&(1+\varepsilon)2L^2+\frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon} (R^{-1}+\varepsilon)d_{\tilde g_s(1)}\bigl(\gamma(0),0\bigr)^2\\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Choosing $\varepsilon<\frac{1}{8}$ and $R^2=R(L)^2>\max \{64,(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}8L^2\}$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
D_{sR}(\gamma)^2
\leq 4L^2
+\frac12D_s(\gamma)^2.
\end{equation}
 and thus since $8L^2\le (1-\varepsilon)R^2$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:consequence.of.iteration}
    D_s(\gamma)^2\le 8L^2\Longrightarrow D_{sR}(\gamma)^2\le 8L^2.
\end{equation}

 By \eqref{eq:estimate.g_s(1)} and \eqref{eq:estimate.g_s(R)}, we have for $1\le r\le R$
\[
D_{s_1r}(\gamma)^2\le (1+\varepsilon)(\frac{v_0^2}{r}+\theta_0^2)\le (1+\varepsilon)(v_0^2+\theta_0^2)\le \frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}D_{s_1}(\gamma)^2\le 2L^2.
\]
Thus $\sup_{s\in [s_1,s_1R]} D_{s}(\gamma)^2\le 2L^2<8L^2$. Applying \eqref{eq:consequence.of.iteration} iteratively gives for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$
\[\sup_{s\in [s_1R^k,s_1R^{k+1}]}D_{s}(\gamma)^2\le 8L^2,\] that is
\[\sup_{s\ge s_1}D_{s}(\gamma)^2\le 8L^2.\]This proves the claim.

label: t:GH_limit_vs_rationality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:GH_limit_vs_rationality}
Let $s_i\to\infty$ be a sequence such that $(M,g_{s_i}(1))\xrightarrow{GH}(X,d)$, and suppose that, on the universal cover,
\[
(\tilde g_{s_i}(t),\tilde\alpha_{s_i}(t))
\xrightarrow{C^\infty}
\bigl(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t)\bigr).
\]
Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item If $(X,d)=\{\mathrm{pt}\}$, then $[\alpha]$ is irrational.
    \item If $[\alpha]$ is rational, then $(X,d)=(S^1,d([\alpha]))$.
    \item If, in addition, $(\tilde g_s(t),\tilde\alpha_s(t))\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ as $s\to\infty$ with no fiber component, then $(X,d)=(S^1,d)$ implies that $[\alpha]$ is rational. Consequently, by (ii), $(X,d)=(S^1,d([\alpha]))$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Step 1}: Setup.

As in Example~\ref{example.noncompact invariant expander}, in local coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^2$, we have $g^*(t) = dv^2 + td\theta^2$ and  $\alpha^*(t)=\sqrt 2 d\theta$. We define $u^*=\sqrt 2\theta\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$ so that $\alpha^* = du^*$. We have the following equivariant convergence:
\begin{center}
    \begin{tikzcd}
  & (\tilde{M},\tilde{g}_{s_i}(1), \tilde\alpha_{s_i}(1), G_{s_i}, p) \arrow[r,  "pt\ eq\ C^\infty"] \arrow[d, "\pi"]
   & (\mathbb{R}^2,g^*(1), \alpha^*(1), G_\infty, p_\infty) \arrow[d,  "\pi_\infty"]\\
  & (M, g_{s_i}(1)) \arrow[r, "GH"]
   & (X,d),
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
where $(X, d)$ is either $(S^1, d)$ or a point and $G_\infty = \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$, respectively, by Corollary~\ref{c:convergence_CFG}. For each $i$, we write $ g_i:= g_{s_i}(1)$, $\tilde g_i:=\tilde g_{s_i}(1)$, $\alpha_i:=\alpha_{s_i}(1)$ and $\tilde\alpha_i:=\tilde\alpha_{s_i}(1)$. Note, for each $i$, there exists $u_i \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$, such that $du_{i} = \tilde\alpha_i$. We normalize these functions such that $u_{i}(0) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets}, we know that $G_i$ acts on the collection of level sets $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$.

\textbf{Step 2}: Passing the action of $G_i$ on level sets to the limit.

Smooth pointed convergence and the normalization $u_i(0)=u^*(0)=0$ give $u_i\to u^*$ in $C^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $\gamma_i\to\gamma\in G_\infty$, then $[\alpha](\gamma_i)=u_i(\gamma_i(x))-u_i(x)\to u^*(\gamma(x))-u^*(x)$. The limit is independent of $x$, so $G_\infty$ acts on the level sets of $u^*$.

\textbf{Step 3}: We prove (i). If $(X,d)=\{\mathrm{pt}\}$, then $[\alpha]$ is irrational.

By Corollary~\ref{c:convergence_CFG}, $G_\infty=\mathbb{R}^2$ which acts transitively on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Thus, for any $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$, there is $\gamma\in G_\infty$ such that $u^*(\gamma(x))-u^*(x)=\lambda$. Let $\gamma_i\in G_i$ be such that $\gamma_i\to \gamma$. Then $u_i(\gamma_i(x))-u_i(x)=[\alpha](\gamma_i)$ converges to $\lambda$ as $i\to\infty$. Since the action of $G_i$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is independent of $i$, the action of $G_i$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is not discrete. By Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets}, $[\alpha]$ is irrational. In particular, we know that if $[\alpha]$ is rational, then $(X,d)=(S^1,d)$.

\textbf{Step 4}: Identifying the $\mathbb{R}$ component of $G_\infty$ when $[\alpha]$ is rational.

By Step 3 and Theorem~\ref{no_fiber_component}, $(X,d)=(S^1,d)$ and the limit $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ has no fiber component. By Corollary~\ref{c:convergence_CFG}, $G_\infty \cong \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$. Since $\alpha^* = \sqrt{2} \, d\theta$, the fiber direction cannot contain a $\partial_\theta$ component, which implies that $\partial_v$ must correspond to the fiber direction. Let $H_\infty = \big\{(\theta,v) \mapsto (\theta,v+v_1) : v_1 \in \mathbb{R} \big\} \le G_\infty$ be the $\mathbb{R}$-subgroup generated by $\partial_v$. We then observe that for any point $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$, if $u^*(x) = r$, the entire orbit $H_\infty \cdot x$ coincides precisely with the level set $(u^*)^{-1}(r)$.

\textbf{Step 5}: We prove (ii). If $[\alpha]$ is rational then $(X,d)=(S^1,d([\alpha]))$.

By Lemmas~\ref{l:collapsing.generators} and \ref{l:zero.pairing.with.fiber}, there exist closed curves $\gamma_i$ and $\sigma_i$ such that $[\gamma_i], [\sigma_i]$ generate $\pi_1(M)$, $L(\gamma_i, g_i) \to 0$, $L(\sigma_i, g_i) \to L(S^1, d)$, and $[\alpha](\gamma_i) = 0$. Since $[\gamma_i], [\sigma_i]$ generate $\pi_1(M)$, Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets} implies that $u_i([\sigma_i](x))-u_i(x)=[\alpha](\sigma_i)=\ell([\alpha])$. By Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets}, the action of $G_i$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is generated by $r\mapsto r+\ell([\alpha])$ which is independent of $i$. Thus by Step 2, the action of $G_\infty$ on $\{(u^*)^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is a subgroup of $\langle r\mapsto r+\ell([\alpha])\rangle$. 
We now show that the action is the full group. Since $d_{g_i}([\sigma_i](x),x)\le L(\sigma_i,g_i)$ is uniformly bounded, passing to a subsequence yields $[\sigma_i]\to \sigma_\infty\in G_\infty$. Thus we have $u^*(\sigma_\infty(x))-u^*(x)=\ell([\alpha])$. Therefore, the action of $G_\infty$ on $\{(u^*)^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is generated by $ r\mapsto r+\ell([\alpha])$. By Step 4, the orbit $H_\infty \cdot x$ coincides with the level set $(u^*)^{-1}(r)$. Thus $S^1$ has length $\ell([\alpha])/\sqrt 2$.

\textbf{Step 6}: We prove (iii).

    Suppose $L=L(S^1,d)>0$. By Lemma~\ref{l:collapsing.generators}, there exist generators $[\gamma],[\sigma]\in \pi_1(M)$ such that for some $s_1>s_0(2L)$ given in Lemma~\ref{l:bounded.generator}, we have $d_{g_{s_1}(1)}([\gamma](0),0)\le 2L$, $d_{g_{s_1}(1)}([\sigma](0),0)\le 2L$. By Lemma~\ref{l:bounded.generator}, we have $d_{g_s(1)}([\gamma](0),0)\le L'$ and $d_{g_{s}(1)}([\sigma](0),0)\le L'$ for any $s\ge s_1$. Then $G_i\ni[\gamma]\to \gamma_\infty\in G_\infty$ and $G_i\ni[\sigma]\to \sigma_\infty\in G_\infty$. Since $[\gamma],[\sigma]$ are generators, the action of $G_i$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ then fully passes to the limit action of $G_\infty$ on $\{(u^*)^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$. Thus if $(g^*(t),\alpha^*(t))$ has no fiber component and $(X,d)=(S^1,d)$, then by the same argument as Step 4, the action of $G_\infty$ on $\{(u^*)^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is discrete and so is the action of $G_i$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$. Thus $[\alpha]$ is rational by Lemma \ref{action.on.level.sets}.

title: Remark
body_md: Theorem~\ref{t:GH_limit_vs_rationality} is an analog of \cite[Proposition~6.2]{lott2010dimensional}. In the 3D Type III Ricci flow with diameter bounds studied by Lott \cite{lott2010dimensional}, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the expander on the universal cover and the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of the blow-down. In our setting, however, this one-to-one correspondence fails because the same expander $(g^*(t), \alpha^*(t))$ can yield different Gromov--Hausdorff limits. Indeed, as shown in Example~\ref{example.noncompact invariant expander}, $(g^*(t), \alpha^*(t))$ can be quotiented by either an $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$ or an $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ group action to obtain the corresponding base limit. The information determining which quotient is realized is precisely encoded in the cohomology class $[\alpha]$, as manifested in Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets} and the proof above.

label: r:S1.not.imply.rational
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{r:S1.not.imply.rational}
       One cannot conclude that $[\alpha]$ is rational merely from the fact that, along a subsequence, the Gromov--Hausdorff limit is $(S^1, d)$ and the limit on the universal cover $(g^*(t+c), \alpha^*(t+c))$ has no fiber component. Indeed, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in\mathbb{R}\}$ may be lost in the limit, allowing a sequence of dense actions to converge to a discrete one. For example, in $(\theta,v)$ coordinates, consider the lattices generated by $(\frac{\sqrt 2}{i^2},\frac{1}{i})$ and $(1,0)$. The corresponding action on $\{(u^*)^{-1}(r):r\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is dense for every $i$, but the lattices converge to the group of integer $\theta$-translations and arbitrary $v$-translations, isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}$, which gives a discrete action in the limit. Thanks to Lemma~\ref{l:bounded.generator}, when full-sequence convergence on the universal cover holds, such pathologies cannot occur.

label: rational.class.alpha.nonzero
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{rational.class.alpha.nonzero}
    Suppose $[\alpha]$ is rational. Furthermore, suppose that there exists a sequence $s_i\to\infty$ such that $(\tilde{g}_{s_i}(t),\tilde{\alpha}_{s_i}(t))\xrightarrow{C^\infty}(\tilde{g}_\infty(t),\tilde{\alpha}_\infty(t))$. Then $(\tilde{g}_\infty(t),\tilde{\alpha}_\infty(t))$ cannot be $(g_{\mathrm{Euc}},0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose for contradiction that $(\tilde g_\infty(t),\tilde\alpha_\infty(t))=(g_{\mathrm{Euc}},0)$. For each $i$, we write $ g_i:= g_{s_i}(1)$, $\tilde g_i:=\tilde g_{s_i}(1)$, $\alpha_i:=\alpha_{s_i}(1)$ and $\tilde\alpha_i:=\tilde\alpha_{s_i}(1)$.
    On $\tilde M$, there exists a function $u_i\in C^\infty(\tilde M)$ such that $\tilde \alpha_i=du_i$. Since $[\alpha]$ is nonzero, the function $u_i:\mathbb{R}^2\to \mathbb{R}$ is surjective. 
    
    Set $\ell=\ell([\alpha])$ and choose $p\in u_i^{-1}(\ell/2)$ and $q\in u_i^{-1}(0)$. By Lemma~\ref{action.on.level.sets}, $u_i([\gamma](q))\in\ell\mathbb{Z}$ for every deck transformation $[\gamma]$. Integrating $du_i=\tilde\alpha_i$ along a curve $c$ from $p$ to $[\gamma](q)$ gives $\ell/2\le L(c)\|\tilde\alpha_i\|_{L^\infty(\tilde g_i)}$. Taking the infimum over these curves and deck transformations yields
    \begin{equation}\label{lower.bound.of.diameter}
        \operatorname{diam}(M,g_i)\ge d_{g_i}(\pi(p),\pi(q))
        \ge \frac{\ell}{2\|\tilde\alpha_i\|_{L^\infty(\tilde g_i)}}.
    \end{equation}
    As $i\to\infty$, smooth pointed convergence to
$(g_{\mathrm{Euc}},0)$ implies that
$|\tilde\alpha_i|_{\tilde g_i}^2\to0$ uniformly on bounded balls.
By Theorem \ref{diameter.bound}, every point of $M$ has a lift
within a fixed distance of the chosen basepoint in $\tilde M$.
Since $\tilde\alpha_i$ and $\tilde g_i$ are deck-invariant,
it follows that
$
\sup_{\tilde M}|\tilde\alpha_i|_{\tilde g_i}^2\to0
$. By \eqref{lower.bound.of.diameter}, this forces $\operatorname{diam}(M, g_i) \to \infty$, directly contradicting the uniform upper bound $\operatorname{diam}(M, g_i) \le C$ from Theorem~\ref{diameter.bound}.

title: Remark
body_md: The argument in Lemma~\ref{rational.class.alpha.nonzero} does not extend to the case where $[\alpha]$ is irrational. In that setting, the action of $\pi_1(M)$ on $\{u_i^{-1}(r):r\in\mathbb{R}\}$ has dense orbits so that there is no contradiction to the diameter bound Theorem~\ref{diameter.bound}.
